DESPERATE RAILROADERS.
Great Excitement Among Laborers at the Reduction of Their Wages-If General-Manager Moxie
Had Been at Wildhorse Last Monday the Texas Pacific Would Have Been an Official Short.
Sr. Louis, January 13.—The story comes up from Texas that the section hands and other laborers on the Texas Pacific railroad are greatly excited over the recent reduction of their wages to $1 15 per day, and that, four days ago, a large party of them stopped the pay-car at a point called Wildhorse, under the impression that it was General-Manager Hoxie's car and that he was aboard of it. They side-tracked it and demanded the delivery of Mr. Hoxie that they might lynch him. When told that that official was not in the car the mob would not believe it, and they piled up wood around the car to fire it, and, as they said, roast Hoxie out. Paymaster Kretz finally made the excited men comprehend that Mr. Hoxie was not present, but they kept the car on the side track two days before they allowed it to go East. It is also said that great dissatisfaction exists at other points along the line, and that a considerable number of mechanics have been discharged from the shops at Marshall. It is also stated that there is to be a general reduction of wages soon. If this is carried out the men say there will be trouble.

Mad Men.
St. Louis, 13.—It is reported from Texas that section hands and laborers on the Texas Pacific, engaged at the reduction of wages, stopped the pay car at a place called Wildhorse and threatened to lynch Paymaster Hoxie, who, they insisted, was aboard. They finally were about to burn the car but were made to understand that Hoxie was not present, but they kept the car side tracked two days before allowing it to proceed. The dissatisfaction is said to be quite general owing to the threatened reductions.
hoxie-wild-horse-1882-01.A9:
A Mob After a Pay-car.
The colored porter, late in the employe of Paymaster Kretz, of the Texas & Pacific Railway, broke a bit of news here Thursday night which was at first not credited, though on investigation it was found that he told the truth. The facts have been kept quiet for the past ten days. At that time Paymaster Kretz went west over the line to settle with the employes of the road. On reaching a station a short distance this side of El Paso the car was halted by an armed lot of laborers who demanded their pay. These men, it appears, had belonged to the grading force and for some reason Mr. Kretz did not have them down on his pay list. The men were considerably excited and threatened destruction to the car, which they detained four or five hours, by which time Paymaster Kretz had convinced them of their error, when the train was permitted to pass on.

METHOD OF RAISING WAGES ON
THE TEXAS.
St. Paul Pioneer-Press.

The pay of employees of the Texas Pacific Railray having been reduced, a mob side-tracked the pay car and proceeded to smoke Manager Hoxie, out, and were only prevented by the paymaster's earnest explanation that he wasn't there. They would raise wages in the Southwest on the same principle they would recover deposits from an exploded bank, by holding the executive head as a hostage and quickening his conscience by an application of hemp.

There is not a railroad man in the United States more "universally" cursed by employes than is Mr. Hoxie. His methods are peculiarly obnoxious, and he enjoys the hatred of nearly every man working under him. Wages are being cut down to almost the little end of nothing, and shops are being decimated while overcrowded with work. Passes are refused all employes, and every mile ridden by them on the road while not on duty has to be paid for at the same rate charged ordinary passengers. Every burden is put upon the men, and no advantage given them. The slightest mistake or neglect subjects the offender to discharge. The other day Mrs. J. J. Frey rode on a passenger train from Carondelet to St. Louis. As she was the wife of a prominent railroad official, and a person known to have a regular "annual," the conductor passed her by without inquiry. A day or two after, he was discharged for failing to demand a ticket from her! The depth of petty meanness, we think, could go no further. In the event of a general strike, as in 1877, we don't think the employes of the Iron Mountain route would stick so closely to their employers as they did at that time. As evidence of how the men feel toward Mr. Hoxie, we give the following, from a Dallas (Texas) special to the Republican of a recent date:

There is great excitement among section hands and other laborers on Texas and Pacific railroad because of the recent circulars issued by Manager Hoxie reducing their wages to $1.15 per day. An exciting scene occurred as a consequence a few days ago at Wild Horse station, about 400 miles west of Dallas, which has been kept from the reporters and the public generally, but now comes out from parties, eye-witnesses to the scene. The pay-car, with Paymaster Kretz and assistant, was making its monthly trip for settlement. A large force was congregated at Wild Horse. The car was mistaken for Hoxie's private car, and Paymaster Kretz was supposed to be Hoxie. The anger of the men at once became uncontrollable. They side-tracked the car and demanded the delivery of Hoxie, that they might lynch him. They would not believe the announcement that he was not on board and piled up wood around the car to set it on fire, and, as they said, roast Hoxie out. Msj. Kretz made a speech and pacified the crowd, and they finally desisted, but kept the car on the side track forty-eight hours, when it was allowed to proceed eastward.

"Will the people of the United States want to see such a spectacle?"

"Well, I rather guess they will," was the reply. "I haven't the slightest doubt of success from that point of view. Why, in this very city I expect to engage the largest and most prominent place of amusement for the exhibition, and am confident of being completely satisfied with the financial result to myself. I don't know what Guiteau's relatives think about it, but they are poor, and it seems to me that after all the abuse they have received from him during the trial, and all they have had to suffer in consequence of his act, they ought to have some recompense. A California Girl in Trouble.

CHICAGO, January 31st.—The Times says: Miss Belle Metzger, of Oakland, Cal., told a sensational story at the police headquarters to-day of some curious adventures. She left Oakland, she said, about two weeks ago, intending to visit friends at Tuson, Arizona. On the train she met a handsome young fellow, who gave the name of Walter H. Chase, and who succeeded in capturing her affections. He induced her to come on with him to Chicago, promising to marry her immediately on their arrival. They arrived here about the end of last week, registering at the Tramont House as W. B. Hart and wife. Chase suggested that they should spend Sunday in seeing the sights about town, and they would get married the next day. He had deposited her satchel, containing $1,400 worth of jewels and $143 in money, in the sale of the hotel. At an early hour Monday, however, he left his affluent wife quietly sleeping, and going to the clerk asked for the satchel. He got it and they looked upon his

Miss Metzger is a light-haired, interesting girl, about 23 years old. Her lover left her absolutely penniless, and her baggage was seized by the hotel authorities on account of her unpaid board bill. The Anti-Polygamy Agitation.

CHICAGO, January 31st.—The committee appointed last week at the anti-polygamy meeting met to-day and organized a movement for communicating with prominent men in various States and Territories regarding the matter.

COLUMBUS (O.), January 31st.—A large anti-polygamy meeting was held here tonight. Governor Neal, of Idaho, delivered a stirring address. Resolutions were adopted memoralizing Congress.

Destruction by Fire.

HAVANA (Ill.), January 31st.—The Mason County Court-house was burned Sunday night. Loss, $25,000; insurance, $5,000.

QUINCY (Ill.), January 31st.—The loss by the brewery fire yesterday was only about $6,000.

GALVESTON (Tex.), January 31st.—All the wires leading out of the city were prostrated by the fire at Houston, in the building occupied by the Postoffice, Texas Bank and Western Union Company. No further particulars are obtainable.

HOUSTON (Tex.), January 31st.—The fire in Telegraph Block last night resulted in $20,000 damages. Some mail matter was destroyed.

Serious Railroad Accident—Three Men Killed and Others Injured.

CHEYENNE (Wyo.), January 31st.—An accident near Fort Steele, Wyoming, last night, on the Union Pacific Railroad, resulted in the death of three men, named Benjamin Hobart, a freight conductor, J. Seeley, a brakeman, and P. Smith, a fireman, and the injury of four others. The pay car, running as a special, ran into the rear of the freight train. The car was badly damaged. Being on its return trip it contained no money. The freight train was just entering a side track when the pay car special swung around a curve and telescoped the caboose.

Diabolical Outrage Promptly Avenaged.

LOGANSPORT (Ind.), January 31st.—Wm. Steele, a tramp, Saturday night stopped at a farm house and asked for supper. Finding the woman, Mrs. Buell, alone, he outraged her and fled. The neighbors caught the fand, bung him, then piled brush about his body, and setting it on fire, burned it past recognition.

A Flendish Fair.

STERLING (Ill.), January 31st.—The village of Rockfalls is in somewhat of an unprobe because of a man and woman named Seymour having beaten, skinned and otherwise brutally misused the seven-year-old daughter of Mrs. Boller, whose husband is in the insane asylum. The little girl was working for the Seymours, but now has been taken away, and is under physicians' care. Twenty or thirty persons last night visited Seymour for the purpose of lynching him, but he escaped with his wife, and diligent search failed to discover them. The methods of cruelty employed upon the innocent child are too diabolical for mention.

Murdered with Pitchforks.

WINONA (Minn.), January 31st.—Robert and John Carroll brutally murdered with pitchforks Titus Hoyt, a respected farmer, with whom their father was in dispute. The three Carrolls, who are a hard set, have been arrested.

Charged with Murder.

NEW OBLEANS, January 31st.—Two white men, McKee and Singlebarre, have been arrested for the murder of Marshal Smith, a colored preacher, at Clinton, La.

A High-tempered Wife.

DISCO (Ill.), January 31st.—Sunday night Mrs. D. W. Miller, becoming involved in a difficulty with her husband, seized an ax and attempted to kill him. Failing in this, she retired to another room, saturated her clothing with kerosene and set fire to her dress. She was burned to death.

Baldwin's Sentence.

TRENTON (N. J.), January 31st.—Oscar L. Baldwin, late Cashier of the Mechanics' National Bank of Newark, appeared before the United States Court to day, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to fifteen years in State Prison.

Stolen Silks Recovered.

JACKSON (Mich.), January 31st.—The $12,000 worth of silks stolen from Camp, Merrill & Camp, at Jackson last Wednesday night, have been found lodged in the office of J. M. Welch, a lawyer, situated a few feet from where they were taken, from a fellow named Thomas, who had an office with Welch, who sold three pieces of silk last Saturday, at Al-

Collision of Trains.

CINCINNATI, January 31st.—The Gazette's Hangling Rock special says: A freight collided with a construction train to-day on the Scioto Valley Railroad. Two men were killed outright, and five badly injured. It is said the freight conductor was running without orders.

Albany, January 31.—There was no organization of the legislature to-day.

Quincy, Ill., January 31.—The loss by the brewery fire yesterday was only about $6000.

Philadelphia, January 31.—The coal operatives in Schuylkill county will suspend mining nine days in February.

Havana, Ill., January 31.—The Mason county courthouse was burned Sunday night. Loss, $25,000; insurance, $5000.

Erie, Pa., January 31.—Master T. S. Plunkett, of the United States steamer Michigan, was drowned to-day while skating.

Petersburg, Va., January 31.—It has been snowing all night and is six inches deep along the Norfolk and Western railroad.

St. Louis, January 31.—Tom Kelly, who is to second Paddy Ryan in his fight with Sullivan next week, left for New Orleans tonight.

New York, January 31.—A dispatch from Paris says Vigneaux, in the second inning tonight, scored 394, beating the best previous score—Shaeffer's 340.

New Orleans, January 31.—Two white men, McKee and Singleberry, have been arrested for the murder of Marshal Smith, a colored preacher, at Clinton, Louisiana.

Stanford, Ky., January 31.—Dr. S. P. Craig died last night from the effects of a blow on the head with a beer glass, administered during a drunken quarrel, Saturday night, by George Pope.

Higginsport, O., January 31.—James Jackson, colored, was stabbed through the heart this evening in a drunken quarrel with Jackson Downs, white. Downs was arrested and the bloody pocket-knife found in his possession.

Galveston, January 31.—All the wires leading out of the city are prostrated by the fire at Houston in the building occupied by the postoffice, Fox's bank and the Western Union Company. No further particulars are attainable.

Trenton, N. J., January 31.—Oscar L. Baldwin, late cashier of the Mechanics National Bank, Newark, appeared before the United States Court to-day and pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to fifteen years in the State prison.

Richmond, Va., January 31.—The House of Delegates, by a vote of 61 to 14, passed the senate joint resolution abolishing the payment of capitation tax as a prerequisite to voting. The question now goes to the people. Five Democrats voted yea.

New Orleans, January 31.—A Houston, Texas, special says the fire, there last night in the Fox building, occupied as the postoffice and the Western Union telegraph office.
New Orleans, January 31.—A Houston, Texas, special says the fire, there last night in the Fox building, occupied as the post-office and the Western Union telegraph office, resulted in damages to the amount of $20,000, but was fully insured. Considerable damage was done to mail matter.

Newark, N. J., January 31.—The gasometer of the Citizens' Gas Company, containing one hundred thousand feet of gas, exploded to-night, knocking the top of the gasometer to pieces, and scattering the debris about the streets. No one was injured and no property adjoining damaged. Damage, $20,000.

Railroad Officials Killed.
National Associated Press.
Waco, Texas, February 8.—Major Washburn, engineer and superintendent of the Missouri Pacific road, and N. W. Stoll, head contractor on construction, were killed in a hand-car accident a few miles below this city last night. Stoll's wife was badly injured, but may recover.

Fires.
National Associated Press.

CINCINNATI, February 8.—Sholteke & Son's furniture factory was destroyed and the Mother of God church damaged by a fire in Covington, Ky., this morning. Loss, $20,000.

BUTTERVILLE, Ind., February 8.—Bewley & Thomas' saw mills burned last night. Loss, $6,000.

MARSHAL, Ill., February 8.—The small village of Casey, six miles west of this place, suffered a disastrous fire last night, eight stores and two residences being destroyed. PHILADELPHIA, February 8.—The stock of Geo. Doll & Co.'s dry and fancy goods importing house was damaged by fire to-night, $3,000; fully insured.

National Associated Press.

Two years before 1873 no man would have dared to say that within two years all those visionary schemes would disappear; that Jay Cook & Co. would break and bank after bank and corporation after corporation fail, until there was a culmination of labor riots in 1877; and yet things looked as bright in 1871 as they do now.

Are these uncalled-for and disgraceful attacks upon ex-President Hayes made for the purpose of aiding Mr. Tilden's prospects for a renomination. It is difficult to find any other reason for them. Mr. Hayes is a private citizen, and there is no possible excuse for starting afresh the old mud batteries upon him. It may seem possible to Mr. Tilden's friends to revive the fraud issue in this way, but if that be their hope, they are destined to be dissappointed. The fraud issue was buried beyond resurrection under the cipher exposures, and the democratic party admitted as much when they declined to renominate Mr. Trilden. Their return to the abandoned issue now shows that they have no live one to take up. —N. Y. Tribune.

Contrary to all English expectations Mrs. Langtry, who has been in the "beauty business" for years past, seems to have made a substantial success on the stage. And according to the critics and letter-writers her success is not owing to her fair face and form so much as to her very positive dramatic talents. About a month ago she made her stage debut in London as Miss Hardcastle in "She Stoops to Conquer." Then she played Pauline in the "Lady of Lyons." Now she plays Blanche Haye in Roberton's comedy of "Ours," and at every step she has gained strength, and her success is more pronounced Her Blanche Hoye, is spoken of as a "creation," and Mrs. Langtry is proving a greater sensation on the stage than she was as the dazzling beauty of the London salons.—Republican.

His pathetic story recalls the touching experience of the discouraged Arkansas settler retreating after a year's trial in the swamps of White River to his old Indiana home. The inspectors of the government monopoly of matches have found an infallible means of detecting "irregular" goods. They get into kitchens on some pretext, and any matches they may find there they try by scratching them violently on the wall. If the matches burn they are contraband, and action is at once brought against the householder.—Le Figaro.

The marriage insurance bubble-buisiness appears to have begun a general collapse in Richmond, Ind. The inducements to policy-holders to get married for a dowery of $500, upon the expenditure of a few handy dollars, appear appear to have been to great for the United States Marriage Dowery association to stand, and the company gas obliged to stop for want of funds to pay the benefits due to members who rushed into matrimony to reap the promised financial reward. The officers of the association retained twenty per cent. of all the money received for running expenses and their own use. They paid some doweries to begin with, but their policy-holders got married too fast. Now suits have been begun against the managers, and some of them have been decided against the officers of the company, some of whom are responsible men. Suits will therefore be brought as fast as marriages mature among the injured.

In Tennessee, a number of colored people have been converted to the Mormon faith, and it is expected that a large number from various Southern states will be forwarded to Utah during the coming summer. prisoners-grabele-1882-01.A1:
The Graball Murder.
The body of Jordan Thompson, colored, was found near Graball last Sunday with the head cut off. Jack Lewis, Adam Felder, Andrew Watts and Lizzie, wife of the murdered man were at once arrested and G. W. Brooks, justice of the peace and A. D. Gee, constable were sent for to hold an inquest, and upon their arrival at Graball, Jake Lewis and Adam Felder were turned over to constable Gee and soon afterward Andrew Watts and Lizzie Thompson were delivered to him; he held them at Grabhll till Monday when they were all taken to Washington by deputy sheriff Spencer and posse. The jury of inquest at Graball returned a verdict that deceased was murdered by the three men arrested. A preliminary examination was held at Washington by Justice Brooks. The complaint was read to the prisoners by the justice and all of them plead not guilty except Jake Lewis, who plead guilty notwithstanding the justice cautioned him. Jake said that he killed Thompson and did not want others to suffer for his act. After hearing all the testimony and there being no evidence against the other parties the justice released them, holding Jake Lewis without bail. The prisoner was placed in charge of constable Gee, who on account of high water was compelled to bring his prisoner round by rail arriving here on the Central Tuesday night and turning his prisoner over to the sheriff at the county jail. Constable Gee reports that while he was asleep at his home in Washington, Monday night, three masked men attempted to rescue the prisoner from the guard, but fortunately Mr. Gee was notified in time to prevent it. The guard think that the parties who attempted the rescue were negroes. During the trial the excitement was very high and guards had to be placed at the doors of the courthouse by the constable to keep the crowd back. Jack claims that he killed Thompson because he threatened his life; no proof of this was elicited at the trial. The killing was done with a club and the subsequent decapitation with an axe.

An old man named Fred. Jaska, residing on the South Side, Milwaukee, beat his son's brains out with an ax helve Monday evening during a family row. The boy was 18 years old, and was named Runheald. After the murder Jaska tried to hang himself, and was suspended when an officer arrived to arrest him. He was cut down, and then stated that his son came home drunk, and a fight ensued. The family is drunken and disreputable, the mother being a House of Correction inmate most of the time.

The Springer bill, defining the law of insanity in criminal cases, provides that no person indicted in the United States Court shall be acquitted on the ground of insanity, idiocy, lunacy, or other unsoundness of mind, except on proof that, at the time of committing the offense, he was laboring under such derangement of reason as either not to know the nature of the act he was doing, or not to know it was unlawful or wrong.

It seems as though woman's suffrage was to become a live issue in American politics. On Bayard's amendment to refer Hoar's resolution, to create a standing committee on woman suffrage, to the Judiciary Committee, the Republicans voted "no." Woman's rights advocates are much encouraged at this, and say the conferring of woman's rights will be one of the most important issues hereafter.

Senatorial elections in France resulted in the complete triumph of the Republicans. Of the seventy-nine seats contested, only thirteen were carried by Monarchists, the remaining sixty-six by Republicans for the greater part pledged to support Gambetta in his scheme for a so-called reform Constitution. Gambetta's popularity with the Parisian masses is fast failing.

The opponents of the attempts to open Indian Territory to the St. Louis and San Francisco Railroad will commence their war by the presentation of a memorial in the Senate protesting against it. One of their principal charges is that the consent of the Choc-taw Nation was obtained by bribery.

william-medly-bear-quarter-1882-02-09.A1:
A Shocking Crime.
NORFOLK, Va., Feb. 11.—A negro named William Medley was tried before Justice Warren, at Bar Quarter Norfolk county, Thursday and committed to jail today for committing a brutal assault upon a little girl five years of age, the daughter of John Weatherfield, a respectable farmer of that section. The child has been terribly injured. The negro was brought to jail by Constable David Sykes, and was with difficulty saved from being lynched by the infuriated residents of Bear Quarter, both whites and blacks.

NORFOLK, VA., February 10.—A negro named William Medley was lodged in the county jail this morning for committing a terrible outrage on a child five years of age, the daughter of John Weatherfield, a respectable farmer of the Bearquarter section of Norfolk county.

Twenty Years in the Penitentiary- Death.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

NORFOLK, VA., June 22.—A negro named William Medley, who attempted to outrage a child in Pleasant Grove district, Norfolk county, last February, was convicted today and sentenced to the penitentiary for twenty years.

Thomas T. Jones, a well-known citizen, died this morning.
